lessons.title: Lesson 1: Naming what you feel
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Name your emotion with a precise word, not just "fine" or "mad".
This lesson builds toward: Three times in one day, you will name what you feel with an exact feeling word and the body clue that goes with it, without using good, bad, fine or mad.
Emotional intelligence starts with self-awareness: knowing what you feel while you feel it. Many of us only use a few words, like good, bad, fine or mad. But "mad" could really be embarrassed, disrespected, worried or tired.
Your body often knows first. A tight jaw, hot face, clenched fists, a knot in your stomach or a racing heart are clues. When you notice one, ask: "What am I feeling right now?" and look for a more exact word.
Naming a feeling clearly helps you calm it and decide what to do. A player who knows "I'm frustrated with myself, not the coach" handles practice differently from one who just feels angry at everyone.
Step by step:
- Notice a body clue: tight jaw, hot face, knot in your stomach.
- Ask: what am I feeling right now?
- Find a more exact word than good, bad or mad.
- Say it to yourself: "I feel ..."
Words to know:
- Emotional intelligence: the skill of noticing and managing your own emotions and understanding other people's.
- Self-awareness: knowing what you feel and why, while it is happening.
Try it now: Three times today, stop and write one exact feeling word and the body clue that went with it (for example: "nervous - fast heartbeat before my shift"). Try not to use good, bad, fine or mad.
You can now notice body clues and name your emotion with an exact word.

check.q: Which is a more exact word for feeling bad before a big test?
check.why: "Nervous" names the exact feeling, which helps you handle it.

check.q: You notice a tight chest and fast heartbeat before your shift. What would you do?
options: Ignore it and hope it goes away
Name the feeling with an exact word, such as worried
check.why: Naming the feeling from your body clue is the first step to managing it.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Finding your triggers
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Identify two situations that set off strong reactions in you.
This lesson builds toward: Looking back at recent strong reactions, you will identify two of your triggers and what each one touches, such as respect or fairness, with a planned response written for each.
A trigger is a situation, word or action that sets off a strong emotion fast: being interrupted, being corrected in front of others, someone being late, a certain tone of voice, losing a close game, feeling ignored.
Triggers often connect to things that matter to you, like respect, fairness or safety, or to past experiences. For someone coming home from prison, being talked down to may hit hard. For a veteran, a sudden loud noise may. That is human, not a flaw.
When you know your triggers, they lose some of their power. You can plan ahead: "When my manager corrects me in front of the team, I will take a breath, say 'got it', and ask to talk after."
Step by step:
- Think of the last two times you reacted strongly.
- Write what happened right before.
- Write what it touched: respect, fairness, safety, being heard?
- Write a plan for next time.
Words to know:
- Trigger: a situation or action that sets off a strong emotion quickly.
- Pattern: something that happens again and again in a similar way.
Try it now: Write your top two triggers. For each, write what it touches (respect, fairness, safety, being heard) and one sentence about how you will respond next time.
You can now name your triggers, see what they touch, and plan a better response in advance.

check.q: What do triggers often connect to?
options: Things that matter to you, like respect or fairness
check.why: Triggers usually touch something you care about deeply.

check.q: Being talked over in meetings always makes you angry. What would you do?
options: Hope it does not happen again
Write it down as a trigger and plan how you will respond next time
check.why: Planning ahead takes power away from the trigger.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Pausing before you respond
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Use the STOP pause to choose your response in a heated moment.
This lesson builds toward: In a heated moment, you will use the STOP pause to choose your response, before you speak or send a message.
Between what happens and what you do, there is a tiny gap. Self-control means making that gap bigger. One easy tool is STOP: Stop. Take a breath. Observe what you feel and what is happening. Proceed with a choice.
In the moment, a few slow breaths, counting to ten, or saying "Give me a minute" buys time. If you are too heated to talk well, it is okay to say "I want to talk about this, but I need ten minutes first" and come back. Coming back is the key part.
Pausing is not the same as bottling up. You still deal with the feeling; you just do it when you can think clearly. Athletes call this staying composed; a calm player makes better decisions late in the game.
Step by step:
- Stop: don't speak or hit send yet.
- Take a slow breath, or three.
- Observe: what am I feeling? What is really happening?
- Proceed: choose what to say or do, or ask for a short break and come back.
Words to know:
- Self-control: choosing what you do even when you feel a strong emotion.
- Composure: staying calm and clear-headed under pressure.
Try it now: Think of a message or comment that made you angry recently. Walk through STOP on paper: what you felt, what was really happening, and what you would say now. Next time it happens for real, use STOP before you respond.
You can now use STOP to pause and choose your response instead of reacting.

check.q: What does the S in STOP stand for?
check.why: STOP starts by stopping before you react.

check.q: A rude text arrives and you start typing an angry reply. What would you do?
options: Send it fast before you change your mind
Stop, take a breath and decide what to say once you are calm
check.why: Pausing lets you choose your response instead of reacting.

chapters.name: Chapter 2: Understanding and working with others

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Listening with empathy
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Listen and reflect back so the other person feels understood.
This lesson builds toward: When someone shares a problem, you will reflect back what they feel and ask an open question, so they say you understood them.
Empathy means understanding what someone else feels and why, even if you would feel differently. You do not have to agree with them to understand them.
Most people listen to reply. Empathic listening means listening to understand. Put the phone down, look at the person, and let them finish. Then reflect: say back what you heard and the feeling you noticed. "So you've been covering extra shifts and nobody noticed. That sounds really frustrating."
Then ask an open question: "What would help?" or "What happened next?" Avoid jumping to advice, comparing ("that's nothing, once I...") or saying "calm down". A coach, a customer service worker, a volunteer leader and a parent all get further when people feel heard first.
Step by step:
- Put distractions away and look at the person.
- Let them finish without interrupting.
- Reflect what you heard and the feeling: "Sounds like ..."
- Ask an open question: "What would help?"
Words to know:
- Empathy: understanding what another person feels and why.
- Reflect: say back what you heard in your own words.
- Open question: a question that can't be answered with just yes or no.
Try it now: In your next real conversation, practice one reflection ("Sounds like you felt ...") and one open question. Afterwards, write what the other person said and how they reacted.
You can now listen to understand, reflect what someone said and felt, and ask an open question.

check.q: What does it mean to reflect back?
options: To change the subject to your own story
To say in your words what the other person feels and why
To repeat the last word they said
check.why: Reflecting back shows the person you understood them.

check.q: A coworker says, "I'm so tired of doing all the cleanup." What would you say first?
options: "Calm down, it's not a big deal."
"Sounds like you feel the work isn't shared fairly. What's been happening?"
check.why: Reflecting the feeling and asking an open question shows empathy.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Handling conflict with "I" statements
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Say what bothers you with a calm "I" statement and a clear request.
This lesson builds toward: Given a real issue with another person, you will say what bothers you with a calm "I" statement and a clear request, using the pattern I feel, when, because, could we.
Conflict is normal on any team, in any family and in any business. Handled well, it solves problems. Handled badly, it breaks trust.
"You" statements sound like blame: "You always leave me to close." People defend themselves and stop listening. "I" statements describe your side: "I feel stressed when I close alone three nights in a row, because I miss my bus. Could we take turns?"
The pattern: I feel [emotion] when [specific action] because [why it matters]. Could we [request]? Stick to one issue, describe actions not character ("you were late twice" not "you're lazy"), and listen to their side using the skills from the last lesson. Look for a solution you can both live with.
Step by step:
- Pick one issue.
- Write: I feel ... when ... because ... Could we ...?
- Choose a calm time and private place.
- Say it, then listen and reflect their side.
- Agree on one next step.
Words to know:
- "I" statement: a way to say how something affects you without blaming the other person.
- Conflict: a disagreement between people who need or want different things.
Try it now: Think of a real issue with a teammate, coworker or family member. Write it first as a "you" statement, then rewrite it as "I feel ... when ... because ... Could we ...?" Read both out loud and notice the difference.
You can now turn a complaint into a calm "I" statement with a clear request, and work toward a shared next step.

check.q: Which part of an "I" statement is the clear request?
check.why: "Could we ...?" asks for a specific change.

check.q: A family member keeps checking your phone. What would you say?
options: "I feel uneasy when my phone is checked, because I want trust. Could we talk about it?"
check.why: A calm "I" statement names your feeling and asks for a change without blame.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Giving and receiving feedback
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Give specific, kind feedback and take feedback without getting defensive.
This lesson builds toward: When giving or receiving feedback, you will give specific, kind feedback and respond to tough feedback without getting defensive, describing actions, not the person.
Feedback helps people grow. Good feedback is specific, about actions, and useful. Instead of "Good job" or "That was bad", say what happened and its effect: "Your summary at the start of the meeting kept everyone on track." "The report had three wrong totals, so the client called twice. Can you double-check totals before sending?"
Receiving feedback is harder. Your first feeling may be to defend yourself. Use STOP, listen to the whole thing, reflect it back, and ask a question: "Can you give me an example?" Say thank you, even if you do not agree yet. Then decide what to use. Athletes who take coaching well improve fastest.
When you get it wrong, repair it. A real apology names what you did, its effect and what you will do differently: "I snapped at you in the meeting. That was embarrassing for you. Next time I'll ask to talk after." Now you are ready for your final task.
Step by step:
- Giving: say the specific action and its effect.
- Add a clear request or a thank-you.
- Receiving: pause, listen fully, reflect, ask for an example, say thank you.
- Repairing: name what you did, its effect and what you will do differently.
Words to know:
- Feedback: information about how someone did, given so they can improve or keep doing well.
- Defensive: quickly protecting yourself from criticism instead of listening.
- Repair: fixing a relationship after a mistake, often with a real apology.
Try it now: Final task: plan and hold one conversation you have been putting off. Before it, write what you feel and what triggered it. In it, pause, reflect what they say, and use one "I feel ... when ... because ... Could we ...?" statement. After it, write what went well and one thing to do differently.
You can now give specific feedback, take feedback without getting defensive, repair a mistake, and handle a hard conversation with emotional intelligence.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Feeling and trigger named Used a vague word such as bad or mad, or no trigger written. Wrote an exact feeling word and what triggered it before the talk. Also named what the trigger touches, such as respect or fairness. Paused before responding Reacted fast or raised their voice. Paused at least once before responding in a hard moment. Asked for a short break and came back to finish the talk. Reflected back Did not check what the other person meant. Reflected back the other person's feeling at least once. The other person said they felt understood. "I" statement Used blaming "you" statements. Used one complete "I feel ... when ... because ... Could we ...?" statement. The request led to a clear next step both agreed on. Review afterwards No review written. Wrote what went well and one thing to do differently. Asked the other person for feedback and noted it calmly. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: Which feedback is about actions, not the person?
options: "Two of the orders went out without labels yesterday."
check.why: Good feedback describes specific actions that can change.

check.q: Your coach says your defense was weak in the last game. What would you do first?
options: Argue that the coach is wrong
Listen, reflect it back and ask for an example
check.why: Listening and asking for an example helps you learn instead of getting defensive.
